text.en: The article on Henderson Island says the island was abandoned in the 17th century, while the article on the Pitcairn Islands says Henderson was probably abandoned before the 16th century and Pitcairn in the 17th or early 18th century. Wikidata gives no years.

caption.en: Modern photo (2000) from Henderson Island in the Pitcairn Islands, by Makemake (German Wikipedia), not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: Mangareva was settled by Polynesians during the first millennium, probably around the year 800. The island was forested and had a large population that traded with other islands by canoe. Between the 10th century and the 15th century the forest was cut down, which had severe consequences for both nature and trade.

text.en: The article on Mangareva gives about 800, but carbon-14 has so far only yielded settlement sites from 1160–1220, and traces of trade exist from about 1000. The article on the Gambier Islands considers it more likely that the islands were settled from the Society Islands around the year 1000.

caption.en: NASA astronaut photograph (2001) of Mangareva in the Gambier Islands, French Polynesia; according to the file page cropped and colour-adjusted. Not from the time of the event. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The Marquesas Islands were settled by Polynesians from western Polynesia, descendants of the Lapita culture. A 2010 study with more precise carbon-14 datings shows that eastern Polynesia was settled late and quickly: first the Society Islands around 1025–1120 and then, in a second wave, the Marquesas Islands around 1190–1290.

text.en: Wikipedia also mentions that archaeological research points to the 10th century, and that older datings have given before the year 100 or around 600. Here the 2010 study is used. Wikidata gives no year.

caption.en: Modern photo (2006) by Sémhur: vegetation at the edge of the road from Atuona to Puamau on Hiva Oa in the Marquesas Islands, looking toward the Baie des Traîtres (Traitors Bay) and the Hanakee rock. Not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: The first Polynesians came to the Society Islands, where Tahiti is the largest island, around the year 1000. According to a 2010 study it happened between about 1025 and 1120, several hundred years later than previously thought. From here the settlement of eastern Polynesia continued.

caption.en: Landscape by Admiral Edward Gennys Fanshawe, dated 24 August 1849: Matavai Bay and Point Venus, Tahiti. A watercolour according to the Commons category, made more than 800 years after the event; it shows the landscape, not the event. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In the later part of the 15th century the chief Piʻilani became the first to bring the whole island of Maui under a single lineage. According to tradition his rule was mostly peaceful. He began building a road around the whole island, the first of its kind in the Hawaiian Islands, which his son completed.

caption.en: Modern photo (2013) by Joel Bradshaw of a corner of Piʻilanihale Heiau in Kahanu Garden near Hana, Maui. The file page does not say who built the heiau or when. Not from the time of the event. Licence: CC0.

summary.en: Roi Mata was a chiefly title in central Vanuatu borne by a long line of chiefs from the 11th century to the 17th century. The best known was the last, who is thought to have lived around the year 1600. His grave on the island of Eretoka, with the bodies of more than 25 people from his retinue, was found in 1967 with the help of local stories and became a World Heritage Site in 2008.

caption.en: Modern photo (2006) of Fele’s Cave on Lelepa island, Vanuatu, not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: In 930 the Icelanders gathered for the first time at the Althing, an open-air assembly on the plain of Þingvellir east of today's Reykjavík. It is regarded as the world's oldest legislative assembly. At the Law Rock (Lögberg) the Lawspeaker sat and presided over the assembly. After Iceland came under the King of Norway in 1262, the Althing lost its legislative power.

caption.en: The Althing at Þingvellir in a romanticised painting by W. G. Collingwood, around 1897, long after the assembly's early days. Not a contemporary image. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In 862 the Byzantine emperor sent the brothers Cyril and Methodius from Thessalonica as missionaries to Great Moravia, at the request of Prince Rastislav. Cyril created the Glagolitic alphabet, the oldest known Slavic alphabet, to translate Greek church texts into Old Church Slavonic. Later the Cyrillic alphabet emerged in Bulgaria and gradually took over there.

Around the year 988, Prince Vladimir the Great was baptised at Chersonesos in Crimea and then had his family and his people baptised in Kiev. The event is known as the Baptism of Rus'. Christianity had, however, begun to spread in Rus' earlier, and the conversion was a long process. The year is disputed.

caption.en: The Christianization of Kievan Rus’ in a painting by Klavdy Lebedev (before 1916), not a contemporary image. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In 785 Abd al-Rahman I, founder of the Emirate of Córdoba, had a large mosque begun. Construction went quickly, partly thanks to reused Roman and Visigothic columns, and was finished in 786–787. The mosque was extended several times until the end of the 10th century. When Castile conquered Córdoba in 1236 it was converted into a cathedral.

caption.en: The Mosque of Córdoba seen from the air. Modern photo (2010). Detail. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

summary.en: The Hanseatic League was a loose association of trading towns that grew up around Lübeck and other north German towns from the end of the 12th century. It never had a formal founding, but historians have often counted from 1159, when Lübeck was rebuilt. At its largest the League comprised almost 200 places from Estonia and Russia to the Netherlands. It was dissolved in 1669.

text.en: Wikipedia says the Hanseatic League has no founding year and mentions 1159 as the traditional starting point, with dissolution in 1669. Wikidata gives 1358 as the beginning and 1862 as the end.

caption.en: Bergen in 1905, with the old Hanseatic quarter across the harbour. One half of a stereo photograph, detail. The photo was taken long after the time of the Hanseatic League. The Library of Congress states no known restrictions on publication.

summary.en: Around the year 232, with an uncertainty of about ten years, the Taupō volcano had its most recent major eruption. It is regarded as New Zealand's largest eruption in the past 20,000 years. A pyroclastic flow moved at nearly the speed of sound and covered the ground within 80 km with ignimbrite, and Lake Taupō became larger. No people yet lived in New Zealand; the Māori came more than 1,000 years later.

text.en: Wikipedia gives the year 232 ± 10, within a wider span of 205–373 from palaeomagnetic dating, and writes that the age is still somewhat disputed. Wikidata gives the year 180.

caption.en: Modern satellite image (uploaded 2005) of Lake Taupō on the North Island, from NASA, not from the time of the event. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Borobudur in Central Java is a Buddhist temple built under the Sailendra dynasty. There are no known written records of its construction, so scholars have dated it by comparing the temple's reliefs with inscriptions from the same period. The temple has nine stacked platforms with a large dome on top and is decorated with 2,672 reliefs and originally 504 Buddha statues. It is the largest Buddhist temple in the world. It was later abandoned and lay hidden for a long time under volcanic ash and jungle, until the wider world learned of it in 1814. Today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

text.en: Wikipedia calls Borobudur a 9th-century temple but also writes that it was built in the 8th century. An estimate of the five stages of construction gives about 780–833. World History Encyclopedia places the end of construction at about 800–825. The years here follow the stages, 780–833.

caption.en: Borobudur near Magelang on Java, aerial photograph by the air division of the Royal Netherlands East Indies Army, date unknown. KITLV. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

summary.en: On 11 May 868 a printed scroll with the Buddhist text the Diamond Sutra was completed. According to the text at the end of the scroll, a man named Wang Jie had it made on behalf of his parents, to be given away freely. It is often regarded as the world's oldest surviving printed book, and it is the oldest print that bears a date, although older prints on paper exist.

caption.en: The frontispiece of the Diamond Sutra from Cave 17 at Dunhuang, printed in 868, ink on paper. Now in the British Library. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The Temple of the Feathered Serpent at Teotihuacan was built around 150–200. It takes its modern name from the images of the feathered serpent, a Mesoamerican deity, that cover the sides of the pyramid. They are among the earliest known images of the feathered serpent, which is often identified with the much later Aztec god Quetzalcoatl.

caption.en: Modern photo (2013) by Diego Delso of La Ciudadela in Teotihuacán, Mexico (file page): a staircase with sculpted heads in a pyramid facade. Not from the time of the temple (about the year 150). Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: Kʼinich Yax Kʼukʼ Moʼ is named in Maya inscriptions as the founder and first ruler of Copán, a major Maya city in present-day Honduras. He ruled from 426 to about 437. On the monuments he is shown with features from Teotihuacan, but strontium isotope analysis of the tomb attributed to him shows that he grew up closer to Copán, at Tikal, and had not himself lived at Teotihuacan.

text.en: The same Wikipedia article gives the start of his reign as 426 in the introduction and as 9 February 427 in the infobox.

caption.en: Modern photo (2017) by Hans Birger Nilsen of the Hieroglyphic Stairway at Copán with Stela M (file page title). The file page gives no dates for the monuments; the picture is not from the founding of the dynasty (about the year 426). Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

summary.en: The Tierra Blanca Joven eruption of Ilopango, where Lake Ilopango lies today, is the largest volcanic eruption in El Salvador in historic times and one of the largest on Earth in the past 7,000 years, rating 6 on the VEI scale. Ash from the eruption in precisely dated ice cores from Greenland shows that it happened in 429–433. It therefore cannot have caused the extreme weather of 535–536, with which it was previously linked.

text.en: Wikipedia gives the year 431 with an uncertainty of two years, that is 429–433, based on dating in ice cores from Greenland.

caption.en: Modern image (2021) by KMTRAGER of Lake Ilopango in El Salvador; the file page states that the TBJ eruption created an 8 × 11 km caldera filled with water. Not from the eruption (about the year 431). Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: Puquios are underground aqueducts near Nazca in southern Peru that are still used to bring fresh water for irrigation and households in the desert. Some archaeologists have estimated that the Nazca people began building them around the year 500. The technique resembles the qanats of Iran and other desert regions.

text.en: The age of the puquios is disputed. Most archaeologists believe they were built before the arrival of the Spanish, and some estimate that construction began around the year 500. Others believe they were built in the 16th century by indigenous people under the Spanish colonists.

caption.en: Modern photo (2015) by Diego Delso of some of the Cantalloc aqueducts near Nasca in Peru; according to the file page there are more than 40, built by the Nasca culture about 1,500 years ago. Spiral-shaped entrances to underground water channels. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: The Plague of Cyprian was a pandemic that afflicted the Roman Empire from about 249 to 262. It is thought to have caused shortages of people for food production and the army, weakening the empire during the Crisis of the Third Century. It is named after Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, who wrote about it. The disease is not known; suggestions include smallpox, measles and a haemorrhagic fever.

text.en: Wikipedia gives two datings: about 249–262 or 251/252–270. The first is shown here.

summary.en: Around the year 270, under King Endybis, the Kingdom of Aksum began minting its own coins. Minting continued until it began to decline in the first half of the 7th century. Metal coins may have been used in Aksum for centuries before centralised minting.

Around the year 300, followers of Anthony the Great, an early Christian monk, founded a monastery at an oasis in the Red Sea Mountains in Egypt's Eastern Desert. The Monastery of Saint Anthony is a Coptic Orthodox monastery and one of the most prominent in Egypt. It has strongly influenced Coptic institutions and monasticism in general, and several patriarchs have come from it.

At about sunrise on 21 July 365 the eastern Mediterranean was shaken by an earthquake centred near Crete, which geologists today estimate at magnitude 8.5 or higher. It was followed by a tsunami that devastated the southern and eastern coasts of the Mediterranean, particularly Libya, Alexandria and the Nile Delta. Thousands died and ships were hurled inland. Many writers of the time referred to the event.

The Lydenburg Heads are seven hollow terracotta heads found together with pottery, iron and copper beads and bone fragments at Lydenburg in South Africa. Charcoal from the find has been radiocarbon dated to about the year 500, one of the earliest dates for an Iron Age settlement in South Africa. They are among the oldest known Iron Age artworks in Africa south of the equator.

caption.en: One of the Lydenburg Heads, a terracotta sculpture. Object from Lydenburg, photographed in 2014 by Nkansahrexford. Full image. Licence: CC BY 3.0.

summary.en: According to tradition, the White Horse Temple in Luoyang is founded in 68 with the support of Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han. The temple honoured two Indian monks and the white horses that, according to the story, carried Buddhist scriptures to China. The monks translated many scriptures while living at the temple.

On the night of 13 December 115 Antioch is struck by an earthquake with an estimated magnitude of 7.5. Antioch, Daphne and Apamea are almost completely destroyed, and a local tsunami damages the harbour at Caesarea Maritima. Emperor Trajan, who was in the city, escaped with minor injuries. The death toll is estimated at about 260,000, an uncertain figure.

In 132 the astronomer and inventor Zhang Heng presents a seismoscope to the Han court, which he claimed could show the direction of a distant earthquake. Once the device was triggered although nobody had felt a tremor. A few days later a messenger reported an earthquake in Longxi, in present-day Gansu, in the direction the device had shown.

caption.en: Model of Zhang Heng's seismoscope (Houfeng Didong Yi) at the Museo Oriental de Valladolid in Spain (the file page category); a model, not the original. Modern photo (2016) by Zarateman. Licence: CC0.

summary.en: In 165–180 an epidemic ravages the Roman Empire, probably smallpox but possibly measles. According to the ancient sources it appeared when Roman soldiers besieged Seleucia in Mesopotamia in the winter of 165–166, and the soldiers carried it home. The death toll is estimated at 5–10 million.

text.en: The source is contradictory about where the first case was: Wikipedia's infobox gives Seleucia as the place where the plague was first reported, but the article text also says that the first documented case was in Smyrna in Anatolia in 165. The point is placed at Seleucia.

caption.en: Peter J. N. Geiger's illustration "Antonine Plague in Rome, 165–180", about 1871 (from Zimmermann, Illustrirte Geschichte des deutschen Volkes, 1873). A later, interpretive depiction of the sick and dying, made more than 1,700 years after the event. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Around 427 the Gupta emperor Kumaragupta I founds the monastery of Nalanda near Rajgir in present-day Bihar. It becomes a Buddhist centre of learning that operates for almost a thousand years, until about 1400. Among those who worked or studied there was the Chinese monk Xuanzang.

caption.en: Ruins of the ancient Nalanda University: a detail from Temple 12. Modern photo (2023) by Sumitsurai; not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: Around the year 499 the astronomer Aryabhata compiles his work the Aryabhatiya in Sanskrit, the only one of his writings to survive. It deals with mathematics and astronomy and divides days, months and years according to the movements of the heavenly bodies. The year 499 has been calculated from the work's own reckoning of time.

text.en: The year 499 is calculated from the work's own reckoning of time and is approximate: the historian Roger Billard estimates that the work was compiled around the year 510. The source does not say where the work was written. Aryabhata called himself a native of Kusumapura or Pataliputra and studied there for some time. Another hypothesis links him to the Ashmaka country.

summary.en: According to the Icelandic sagas, Erik the Red was banished from Iceland and used the time to explore the southwest coast of Greenland, around the year 982. A few years later he returned with settlers.

text.en: The year comes from Icelandic sagas that were written down much later. Lex states that Erik was banished around 980.

caption.en: Modern photo (2009) of the farms at Qassiarsuk on the shores of Tunulliarfik Fjord, Greenland, taken from a helicopter, by Algkalv, not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY 3.0.

summary.en: Around 985 Norse settlers from Iceland came to southern Greenland. Erik the Red founded the farm of Brattahlíð in the Eastern Settlement, and others settled in the surrounding fjords and further north near present-day Nuuk. Norse Greenland lasted for about 450 years.

text.en: The year is based on Icelandic written sources (sagas). SNL's article on Erik gives 984–986.

caption.en: Satellite image (ASTER, 2016) of the area around Qassiarsuk, Greenland; the file page states that the first Norse settlement in Greenland was at Brattahlid (now Qassiarsuk). NASA, METI, AIST and Japan Space Systems, not from the time of the event. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In 1124 Arnald was consecrated as the first bishop of the Greenlanders, with the support of the Norwegian king Sigurd the Crusader. The bishop's seat became the great farm of Garðar, the largest farm in Greenland.

text.en: The sources agree that Arnald was consecrated in 1124. Wikipedia writes that he arrived in Greenland in 1126.

caption.en: Modern photo (2008) of Igaliku in southern Greenland, the place where Garðar, the Norse bishop's seat, once lay, by Svickova. Not from the time of the event; the sheep are modern. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In 1261 the Norse Greenlanders submitted to King Haakon Haakonsson and became liable to pay taxes to Norway. In return, the king probably promised to make sure that ships continued to sail to Greenland.

The more northerly of the two Norse settlements, the Western Settlement, became deserted in the second half of the 14th century, about half a century before the Eastern Settlement. There were probably several causes: a colder climate, isolation and a small population.

text.en: SNL writes that contemporary sources describe the settlement as deserted in the middle of the 14th century and that the most recent archaeological dates are from the second half of the 14th century. Lex gives the end of the 14th century. Wikipedia gives 1350 at the latest in one article and around 1360 in another.

summary.en: Life in the larger Eastern Settlement ebbed away during the 15th century, around 1450 according to several sources. The causes are thought to be several at once: a colder and more unstable climate, worn-out pastures, changing trade in Europe and a population of only a few thousand.

text.en: Lex gives the first half of the 15th century or around 1450, SNL around 1450 with the most recent dates from the middle of the 15th century. Wikipedia gives 1450–1500.

caption.en: Modern photo (2014) by jtstewart of Hvalsey Church in Greenland, seen from inside the ruin; two visitors can be seen. The church stood in the Eastern Settlement. Not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

summary.en: In 1408 two Icelanders were married in Hvalsey Church. A letter about the wedding, written the following year, is the last surviving written sign of life from the Norse settlements in Greenland. The ruin of the church is the best preserved from the Norse period.

caption.en: Modern photo (2014) by jtstewart of the ruin of Hvalsey Church in Greenland. Not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

summary.en: The Royal Frankish Annals describe the peace of 811 between the Danish king Hemming and Charlemagne. Among the Danish magnates who confirmed the peace at the River Eider is an Osfrid of Scania. It is the first time Scania is mentioned in writing.

text.en: Only Swedish Wikipedia says that 811 is the first time Scania is mentioned. English Wikipedia quotes the annals' list of names, including Osfrid of Schonen. Den Store Danske only says that from the 9th century there are statements that Scania belonged to the Danish realm that was then taking shape.

summary.en: Around the year 1000 the town of Lund grows up in Scania, which then belonged to Denmark. Lund soon becomes a centre of Danish royal power and of the Church, with Denmark's most important mint and, from around 1060, a bishop's seat.

text.en: Den Store Danske and Nordisk familjebok say around the year 1000. English Wikipedia says that archaeologists date the founding to around 990, and that before the 1980s the town was thought to have been founded around 1020.

summary.en: An archdiocese for all the Nordic countries is established with its seat in Lund. Asser (Asker) becomes archbishop and primate of the whole North, including the Faroe Islands, Iceland and Greenland.

text.en: Den Store Danske and Wikidata give 1103. Nordisk familjebok says that Asker became archbishop in 1104.

summary.en: Archbishop Eskil consecrates the cathedral's high altar. The first altar in the crypt had been consecrated as early as 1123. The church is a Romanesque basilica built of Scanian sandstone.

caption.en: Lund Cathedral today. Photo: Kallekn, 2007. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: In 1332 all of Scania was pledged to a count of Holstein. The Scanians rose up and submitted to the Swedish king Magnus Eriksson. The link was best described as a personal union: the same king, but Scania did not become part of the Swedish realm. In 1360 the Danish king Valdemar Atterdag took Scania back.

text.en: Nordisk familjebok says the population rose against the count and submitted to Magnus Eriksson, who then had to pay the count for his claims. The Swedish Wikipedia says the archbishop asked Magnus to take over Scania, that a Swedish army entered in November 1332 and that the pledge was bought on Magnus's behalf, except for the hundreds of Bjäre and Norra Åsbo, which he bought from Valdemar Atterdag in 1341. The term personal union is used by Nordisk familjebok ("närmast ett slags personalunion") and Store norske leksikon. Wikipedia describes Scania as a further kingdom with its own laws and coinage, and Lex.dk writes that Scania was not incorporated into Sweden.

summary.en: Envoys from Sweden asked the Frankish emperor Louis the Pious for missionaries, and he sent the monk Ansgar to the trading town of Birka in Lake Mälaren. King Björn received him well. Ansgar stayed about six months, and a small Christian congregation was formed, led by Herigar, the chief official of Birka.

text.en: The English Wikipedia says Ansgar arrived in 829. The Swedish Wikipedia says he preached at Birka around 829–831. The information is based on Rimbert's Life of Ansgar.

summary.en: In 1164 Pope Alexander III created a separate church province for Sweden with its archbishop's seat at Uppsala. Until then the Swedish bishops had been under the Archbishop of Lund. The first archbishop was the Cistercian monk Stephen. The seat was at Old Uppsala until Archbishop Folke (1274–1277) moved it to Aros, today's Uppsala.

At Kalmar in 1397, Denmark, Norway and Sweden agreed to have one and the same king. The union was the work of Queen Margaret, and Eric of Pomerania was crowned at Kalmar on 17 June 1397. The union effectively ended when Gustav Vasa was elected King of Sweden in 1523.

Between 1003 and 1010 the Chola king Rajaraja I has a great Hindu temple to Shiva built in Thanjavur in southern India. It is one of the largest Hindu temples and a classic example of Tamil architecture. Today it is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site "Great Living Chola Temples".

caption.en: The Brihadisvara Temple in Thanjavur today. Photo: Shajinss. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: Jiaozi, promissory notes that came into use in Chengdu, are regarded by numismatists as the first paper money in history. When several merchant houses went bankrupt, the state took over the printing and set up its own note office in 1023. In 1024 the first series of government notes with fixed denominations was issued.

text.en: The source says that jiaozi arose in Chengdu, the capital of Sichuan, but does not state explicitly where the government note office was. The place is therefore given as approximate.

summary.en: In 1052 Fujiwara no Yorimichi turns his family's country villa at Uji into a Buddhist temple. Many in Japan then believed that 1052 was the first year of mappō, the "decline of the Dharma", the last and worst of Buddhism's three ages. The belief led many to turn to Pure Land teaching.

caption.en: Modern photo (2010) by Oilstreet of the Phoenix Hall at Byōdō-in in Uji, Kyoto Prefecture. The file page gives the year 1059 for the hall. Not from the time of the event (1052). Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: In 1065 the Nizamiyya is founded in Baghdad, one of the first Nizamiyya schools. It counts among the most important centres of learning of the Abbasid era. Several well-known jurists worked there, among them al-Ghazali.

In 1069–1070 Yusuf, born in Balasagun, writes the Kutadgu Bilig and presents it to the prince of Kashgar in the Kara-Khanid Khanate. For this he receives the title Khass Hajib. The text gives a picture of life and thought in the Kara-Khanid Khanate.

text.en: The place is Kashgar, where the work was presented. The source does not say where it was written. The author was born in Balasagun, near present-day Tokmok in Kyrgyzstan.

summary.en: On 15 March 1079 the Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah I introduces a new solar calendar, on the recommendation of a group of astronomers at the imperial observatory in the capital, Isfahan. One of them was Omar Khayyam. Variants of the calendar are still used in Iran and Afghanistan.

In 1088 the Chinese official and scholar Shen Kuo publishes the Dream Pool Essays, written on his estate near Zhenjiang. In it he is the first to describe the magnetic needle compass and the difference between magnetic and true north. The book also describes Bi Sheng's movable type.

In the capital Kaifeng the official and engineer Su Song builds an astronomical clock tower about twelve metres high, driven by water and fitted with an early escapement. A wooden model is finished in 1088, the bronze parts are cast by 1090 and the whole tower is complete in 1094. His book about the tower, with 47 illustrations of the mechanism, is written in 1092.

caption.en: Drawing of Su Song's astronomical clock tower from his book. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Construction of the Buddhist stupa of Shwezigon begins in 1059–1060 under King Anawrahta, founder of the Pagan kingdom, and is completed in 1102 under his son Kyansittha. The round, gilded stupa became a model for Burmese stupas. It has been damaged by earthquakes and restored several times.

caption.en: Modern photo (2010) by DIMMIS of the Shwezigon in Bagan, Myanmar. Not from the time of the event (construction began 1059). Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: Korea's first printing blocks of the Buddhist canon burned in 1232 during the Mongol invasions. King Gojong had a new set carved: the work began in 1237 and took twelve years. The 81,352 wooden blocks, the oldest complete version of the Chinese Buddhist canon, are kept today at Haeinsa temple.

text.en: The place is Haeinsa temple, where the blocks are kept today. The source does not say where they were carved. The court was then on Ganghwa Island, where the capital had been moved because of the Mongol invasions. The source says the work took twelve years, so the end year is approximate.

caption.en: The Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks on their shelves at Haeinsa temple in South Korea, photographed in 2022. Photo: Bernard Gagnon. Licence: CC0.

summary.en: In 1238 Si Inthrathit makes the city of Sukhothai, in present-day north-central Thailand, the capital of an independent Thai kingdom. The kingdom remains independent until 1438, when it comes under the neighbouring kingdom of Ayutthaya. The ruins of the capital are today a historical park.

A great wooden Buddha was completed in Kamakura in 1243 but was damaged by a storm in 1248. According to the temple's own records, the bronze statue that replaced it dates from around 1252. Including its base it is 13.35 metres tall and weighs about 93 tonnes.

caption.en: The Great Buddha of Kamakura, photographed in 2017. Photo: Suicasmo. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: Around 1250 King Narasingha Deva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty has a temple to the sun god Surya built on the coast at Konark. The temple is built of stone in the shape of a giant, ornamented chariot. It is regarded as the high point of Kalinga architecture.

caption.en: Modern photo by Joydeep of a wheel carved in stone on the Konark Sun Temple in Odisha; the file page states that the temple was built in the 13th century. The file date (2025) is probably the upload, not the time of the photo. Not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: The astronomer Nasir al-Din al-Tusi convinces the Mongol ruler Hülegü that new astronomical tables are needed. Construction of the observatory at Maragheh begins in 1259 and takes three to five years, with al-Tusi as director. Hülegü becomes the first ruler to fund an observatory through a religious endowment, a waqf.

On 25 September 1303 the province of Shanxi in Yuan China is struck by one of the deadliest earthquakes in Chinese history. Historical records give between 170,000 and 270,000 dead. In two nearby towns every major temple and school collapsed, and landslides changed the landscape.

text.en: The figures differ. Historical records usually give 170,000, over 200,000 or 270,000 dead. The same source estimates the magnitude both at 7.6 and at 8.0. In 2018 the epicentre was moved about 60 km north, from Hongtong to the Lingshi area, and the newer location is shown here.

summary.en: Some time between 1307 and 1313 a mausoleum is built for the Ilkhan Öljaitü in his capital, Soltaniyeh, in north-western Iran. The double-shelled main dome is almost 25 metres across and one of the largest brick domes in the world. Since 2005 the building has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

caption.en: Modern photo (2007) by Fulvio Spada from the Oljeitu Mausoleum (Gonbad-e Soltaniyeh) in Soltaniyeh: an interior vault with decoration. Not from the time of the event (1307). Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

summary.en: In 1336 the brothers Harihara I and Bukka Raya I found a Hindu empire in southern India. Its capital, Vijayanagara, at present-day Hampi, remains the capital until 1565, when it is abandoned. The ruins are today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

caption.en: Modern photo (2015) by Aleksandr Zykov from Vijayanagara (Hampi) in Karnataka; the file page does not give the name or age of the building, and the picture does not show the city at the founding of the empire in 1336. Not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

summary.en: At two cemeteries in the Chüy Valley near Lake Issyk-Kul, gravestones with Syriac inscriptions give the name, year of death and often the cause of death. They show a peak of deaths from "pestilence" in 1338–1339. DNA from the teeth of seven of the dead, studied in 2022, contains the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis of a strain that was the direct ancestor of the Black Death strains in Europe and the Middle East.

text.en: Researchers disagree about what the finds mean. Some see the graves as the start of the pandemic. According to others, also cited by the source, they point to a small, sporadic outbreak passed from rodents to humans without wide spread. The cemeteries are at Kara-Djigach and Burana. The point on the map is the Burana Tower.

summary.en: In July 1377 a Korean Buddhist anthology, Jikji, is printed with movable metal type at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju. It is the world's oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type, as UNESCO confirmed in 2001. The surviving part is now in the National Library of France in Paris.

caption.en: Two facing pages (folios 4v–5r) of the Jikji from 1377, in the National Library of France in Paris, which digitised the book. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Around 1400 Parameswara, also called Iskandar Shah, king of Singapura, founds a new realm at Malacca on the west coast of the Malay Peninsula. During the 15th century its capital becomes one of the most important transshipment ports of its time. Malacca also becomes a centre of Islam and of the Malay language.

text.en: Around 1400 is the conventional date, but earlier dates for the founding have also been proposed. Malay and Portuguese sources also give different accounts of the fall of Singapura and its last king.

summary.en: The name Stockholm appears for the first time in two Latin letters from 1252, signed by Birger Jarl. Birger Jarl is traditionally regarded as the founder of the city.

text.en: Wikidata gives 1187 as the year Stockholm was founded. That date comes from the Visby Chronicle, which according to Swedish Wikipedia was only written down around 1410 and is disputed. Shown here is the first certain mention, 1252.

summary.en: In 1477 Archbishop Jakob Ulfsson received a papal bull from Sixtus IV allowing a place of learning in Uppsala modelled on Bologna. Teaching began that autumn. Uppsala University is the oldest university in the Nordic countries.

From the 1220s to the 1440s Mayapan was the political and cultural capital of the Maya on the Yucatán Peninsula. The city had 15,000–17,000 inhabitants and more than 4,000 buildings inside its wall. According to 16th-century sources it was ruled by the Cocom family, and other noble families had to send members there. In 1441 a nobleman of the Xiu family led a revolt against the Cocom.

caption.en: Modern photo (2013) by Arian Zwegers of El Castillo, the Temple of Kukulcan, at Mayapán in Yucatán. According to the file page Mayapán was the political and cultural capital of the Maya in the Yucatán from the 1220s to the 1440s. Not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: The Dresden Codex is a Maya book from the region around Chichén Itzá, written in Maya script on paper made from fig bark and folded like a concertina. It contains astronomical and astrological tables, for example on conjunctions of planets, as well as information on religion, the seasons and illness. The text is based on an original that was three or four hundred years older.

text.en: Wikipedia dates the book to about 1200–1345 but also says that it was long thought to be from the 11th or 12th century. In 2018 the Maya Codex of Mexico (formerly called the Grolier Codex) was shown to be about a hundred years older, so the Dresden Codex is no longer the oldest known book from the Americas.

caption.en: Pages 6 to 8 of the Dresden Codex, a Maya book that the file page dates to about 1200. A photograph or scan of the book. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Abbot Suger had the abbey church of Saint-Denis north of Paris rebuilt. The new choir was built in 1140–1144 and is often regarded as the first building with all the features of Gothic architecture. Large stained-glass windows that filled the church with light then became typical of Gothic architecture.

Gerard of Cremona in Italy travelled to Toledo to learn Arabic so that he could read Ptolemy's astronomical work, the Almagest. His Latin translation from the Arabic, made around 1175, became the most widely known in Western Europe before the Renaissance. He also translated works such as Euclid's geometry and is regarded as the most important of the 12th-century translators in Toledo, who made Arabic and Greek knowledge of astronomy and medicine available in Latin.

On 9 August 1173 the foundations were laid for the bell tower of Pisa Cathedral. The foundations were only three metres deep in soft, unstable ground, and in 1178, when construction had reached the second floor, the tower began to sink. Work then stopped for the better part of a century, and the tower was not completed until the 14th century. The lean remains to this day.

Leonardo of Pisa, who was later called Fibonacci, wrote the arithmetic book Liber Abaci in Latin in 1202. It was one of the first books in Western Europe to describe the Hindu–Arabic numeral system with ten digits and place value, and it is best known for introducing that system and the Arabic numerals in Europe. Leonardo had learned the method as a young man in Bugia in North Africa, where his father worked at the customs house for the merchants from Pisa.

In 1252 the Republic of Florence first struck the gold florin, containing about 3.5 grams of almost pure gold. The coin was accepted across Europe and was used for large transactions such as dowries, international trade and taxes. It was struck without significant change until 1533. Its name comes from the city's floral emblem, which appears on the coin.

The banker Enrico Scrovegni in Padua had a chapel built next to his palace and commissioned the Florentine painter Giotto to decorate it. Giotto and his team covered all the walls and the ceiling with frescoes of the lives of Christ and the Virgin Mary and a large Last Judgement. The frescoes were completed around 1305, the year the chapel was consecrated.

After a conflict between the papacy and the French king, the Archbishop of Bordeaux was elected pope as Clement V. He refused to move to Rome and in 1309 moved his court to Avignon. Seven popes in a row, all French, lived there instead of in Rome. Gregory XI left Avignon in 1376 and arrived in Rome in January 1377. Shortly afterwards the Church split, and a second line of popes in Avignon is today regarded as illegitimate.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 1376 as the end year, when Gregory XI left Avignon, while Wikidata gives 1377. Wikipedia itself mentions that he arrived in Rome in January 1377.

summary.en: Bad weather came in the spring of 1315, and harvests failed until the summer harvest of 1317. The famine struck most of Europe, east to Poland and south to the Alps. Weakened animals fell ill, and the numbers of sheep and cattle fell by as much as 80 per cent. The famine ended the growth that had lasted since the 11th century and was the first of several great crises in 14th-century Europe.

On 18 October 1356 Basel was struck by the most significant earthquake in the recorded history of Central Europe, with a magnitude between 6.0 and 7.1. Torches and candles fell over and set the wooden houses on fire, and the town within the walls was destroyed by the blaze. About 300 people died in Basel, and all major churches and castles within 30 kilometres of the town were destroyed. The seismic crisis lasted a year.

On 27 July 1377 the Great Council of the Republic of Ragusa, now Dubrovnik, decided that merchants, sailors and goods from infected areas could not enter the city until they had spent a month in isolation on uninhabited islands outside the city. The 30-day isolation was called the trentino. When Venice extended the period to 40 days in 1448, the measure got the name quarantine, from the word for forty.

Salisbury Cathedral in England has a large, iron-framed mechanical tower clock without a dial. It is thought to date from about 1386, when a clock is mentioned in a document, and it is a well-preserved example of the earliest type of mechanical clock. It has been called the oldest working clock in the world. The clock was meant to strike a bell at set times. It was rediscovered in 1928 and restored to working order in 1956.

text.en: The source itself says that other clocks make the same claim to be the oldest, among them the clock in Beauvais Cathedral. It is also disputed whether the surviving clock is the one mentioned in 1386: at a symposium in 1993 most participants voted for it being the original, but roughly a third voted for a much later date.

summary.en: Serpent Mound in present-day Ohio is a 411-metre-long earthwork shaped like a snake, the largest known serpent effigy mound in the world. Charcoal found in 1996 was dated to around 1070, in the time of the Fort Ancient culture. Radiocarbon dating in 2014 instead suggested that the Adena culture built the mound around 300 BC and that it was repaired or rebuilt around 1100.

text.en: Researchers disagree about who built the mound. The 2014 dating, which was corroborated in 2019, points to the Adena culture around 300 BC with a rebuilding around 1100. The archaeologist Brad Lepper argues that the samples were unreliable and that the Fort Ancient culture built the mound.

caption.en: Aerial view of the Great Serpent Mound in Ohio, retouched (brightened and with enhanced contrast) according to the file page, from an archive of March 2002 by Timothy A. Price and Nichole I. A modern image, not from the time of the event. The file page attributes the mound to the Adena culture. Licence: CC BY 2.5.

summary.en: Moundville on the Black Warrior River in present-day Alabama was inhabited by the Mississippian culture from around 1000. Around 1150 its leaders began turning the site into a regional centre, a chiefdom. The site has 29 platform mounds around a rectangular plaza. From around 1300 the site was used more as a religious and political centre than as a town, and by around 1500 most of it was abandoned.

caption.en: Modern photo (2010) of the plaza and surrounding mounds at Moundville Archaeological Park in Alabama, seen from the top of Mound B, by Altairisfar (Jeffrey Reed), not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: Casa Grande in present-day Arizona preserves the remains of buildings from the Classic Period of the Hohokam culture, around 1150–1450. The largest building has four storeys and is built of damp earth in layers that were left to dry. The people of the Sonoran Desert who built it farmed the Gila Valley with large-scale irrigation and had extensive trade connections. The building may have been abandoned by around 1450.

caption.en: Modern photo (2006) of the Casa Grande Ruins in Arizona, by Greg Hume, not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: Around the start of the 13th century the Incas founded a small city-state in Cusco in the Andes. According to the Incas' own accounts, Manco Capac was its first ruler. Through war and peaceful assimilation the Kingdom of Cusco grew over time into the Inca Empire, which existed from 1438 to 1533.

text.en: Wikipedia says around the start of the 13th century, while Wikidata gives 1197.

caption.en: Portrait "Manco Capac, First Inca" (oil painting, between 1750 and 1800) from the series Fourteen Portraits of Inca Kings at the Brooklyn Museum. A later portrait, made more than 500 years after the event (1200); it is not a contemporary depiction. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: At Caguana in Utuado, Puerto Rico, the Taíno built ceremonial ball courts, by estimates around 1270. About 13 ball courts and plazas have been identified. They are lined with stone monoliths bearing the largest concentration of petroglyphs in the Antilles, among them the fertility goddess Atabey. The layout of the site appears to follow events in the sky, and many of the carvings show the moon, stars and planets.

caption.en: Modern photo (uploaded in 2006) by Jbermudez (English Wikipedia): the park at the Caguana Ceremonial Center (Parque Ceremonial Caguana) in Puerto Rico. Not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY 2.5.

summary.en: Researchers have radiocarbon dated about 150 samples of dead plants with roots intact that had lain beneath ice caps on Baffin Island and Iceland. According to Miller et al. (2012), they show that cold summers and ice growth began abruptly between 1275 and 1300, with a substantial intensification in 1430–1455. This may have been the start of the Little Ice Age, a period of colder climate that was most pronounced around the North Atlantic.

text.en: When the Little Ice Age began is disputed. It is often dated from the 16th to the 19th century, but some researchers count from about 1300, and Wikidata gives 1303.

caption.en: Aerial photo (2013) by NASA/Michael Studinger of an outlet glacier of the Penny Ice Cap and a tributary glacier of Coronation Glacier on Baffin Island, Nunavut, Canada. A modern photo, not from the time of the event. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: According to the Relación de Michoacán, the leader Tariácuri gathered the communities around Lake Pátzcuaro in present-day Mexico into one strong state. Around 1300 he undertook the first conquests and ruled from Pátzcuaro himself. When he died around 1350, his lineage controlled all the major centres around the lake. The Purépecha Empire became in time the second-largest state in Mesoamerica and lost its independence to the Spanish in 1530.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the empire says that Tariácuri ruled from Pátzcuaro around 1300, but the article on the town says that Pátzcuaro was founded in the 1320s. Wikidata gives 1300 for the start of the empire.

caption.en: Modern photo (2013) by LBM1948 of a yácata pyramid at Tzintzuntzan in Michoacán, with the area around Lake Pátzcuaro in the background. Not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: The Codex Zouche-Nuttall is one of about 16 manuscripts from Mexico that are entirely pre-Columbian in origin. It was probably made in the 14th century from 47 pieces of animal skin, folds like a screen and is painted on both sides with Mixtec pictography. It records the genealogies, alliances and conquests of 11th- and 12th-century rulers of the small Mixtec kingdom of Tilantongo in Oaxaca, especially under the warrior Eight Deer Jaguar Claw.

caption.en: Modern photo (2010) by Szilas of the Codex Zouche-Nuttall, a pre-Columbian Mixtec screenfold book made of deerskin, on display at the British Library in London. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: The Templo Mayor was the main temple of the Mexica in Tenochtitlan, now Mexico City. It was dedicated both to the war god Huitzilopochtli and to the rain god Tlaloc and was seen as the centre of the universe. The first of seven temples on the site was built in 1325 or shortly afterwards, and the second existed by 1375. The largest expansion took place in 1454, and the Spanish destroyed the temple in 1521.

caption.en: First page of the Codex Mendoza (about 1541): the founding of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan. Colours restored and levels adjusted by a Commons user in 2021. Made more than 200 years after the event (1325). Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Between late December 1493 and early January 1494, on his second voyage, Columbus founded La Isabela on Hispaniola, the first stable Spanish settlement in the Americas. The same year La Isabela was struck by the first known epidemic to spread from Europe to the Americas. The event is an early example of the Columbian exchange: plants, animals and diseases carried between the Americas and Europe, Africa and Asia. Diseases from the Old World contributed to an 80–95 per cent fall in the Indigenous population of the Americas.

text.en: Wikipedia says that La Isabela was founded between late December 1493 and early January 1494. Wikidata gives 8 December 1493.

caption.en: Modern photo (2019) by Mariordo of La Isabela Historical and Archaeological National Park in Luperón, Dominican Republic. Not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: In the autumn of 1347 a ship carrying the plague came to Alexandria. In September 1348 the plague reached Cairo, which was then the largest city in the Mediterranean region and larger than any city in Europe. About 200,000 people, a third of the city’s inhabitants, died there, and several quarters lay empty during the following century. The plague then returned to Egypt again and again, 58 times between 1347 and 1517 according to the source.

In 1377 Ibn Khaldun wrote the Muqaddimah, the introduction and first book of a planned world history, the Kitab al-ʿIbar. He begins by pointing out the common mistakes of historians, such as partisanship and over-confidence in their sources, and then sets out a theory of how societies rise and decline. Best known is the concept of ʿasabiyyah, group feeling or social cohesion. Already in his lifetime the Muqaddimah was regarded as a work in its own right, and some scholars today see it as the first work of social science.

The Mutapa Empire was a Shona state on the northern part of the Zimbabwean Plateau, between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers. According to Shona oral tradition the state was founded by Mutota, an elephant hunter who conquered Dande and built a capital with a stone enclosure, and his son Matope expanded it. Historians think the tradition compresses several generations of rulers and date the state’s formation to the 14th and 15th centuries.

text.en: Wikidata gives 1430 as the year the state was founded and 1760 as the year it ended. Wikipedia says that the historians David Beach and Innocent Pikirayi date its formation to the 14th and 15th centuries, and that Mutota may have been a symbolic figure, since he is not mentioned as the founder in traditions recorded before the 1860s. According to the historian Stan Mudenge, the break-up around 1760 is difficult to verify. The dates here are therefore approximate.

summary.en: Around 705 a trading place is founded on the Ribe river in south-west Jutland. Craftsmen work on divided plots, and trade goes mainly to north-west Europe, for example Dorestad in today’s Netherlands. Ribe is regarded as the oldest town in Denmark that still exists.

text.en: Lex states that the trading place was founded around 705 and that the oldest traces date from 704–710. English Wikipedia says that Ribe was a centre of trade in the early 8th century, and Wikidata gives the 8th century.

summary.en: King Harald Bluetooth has a large runestone raised at Jelling in memory of his parents, Gorm the Old and Thyra. The inscription says that Harald won all of Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian, and the stone bears an image of Christ. The stones, the burial mounds and the church at Jelling became a World Heritage Site in 1994.

text.en: The stone is hard to date. Lex places it after Harald’s baptism around 965 and before his death, at the latest in 987. Swedish Wikipedia says it was probably raised between 960 and 985.

summary.en: In 1167 Bishop Absalon begins building a castle on an islet off the settlement of Havn, according to the chronicler Saxo to fight piracy. Remains of the castle survive beneath Christiansborg Palace. The settlement grows into an important trading place and in time becomes Copenhagen.

text.en: The sources differ on when the settlement is first mentioned. Swedish Wikipedia says that Havn is mentioned in 1043. According to Lex, the oldest written source naming Copenhagen is a papal letter from 1186, and Saxo’s wording may mean that a castle already stood there before 1167. Wikidata gives 1167 as the year the city was founded.

summary.en: In 1241 King Valdemar II issues a law for Jutland and Funen with the surrounding islands. According to its preface, it was given at an assembly in Vordingborg with the realm’s magnates and bishops. The preface begins with the words “Med lov skal land bygges” (with law shall the land be built).

On 1 June 1479 the University of Copenhagen is inaugurated at a ceremony in the Church of Our Lady. In 1475 King Christian I had received permission from Pope Sixtus IV to found a university. It is the oldest university in Denmark.

On 7 June 1494 Portugal and Castile signed a treaty at Tordesillas on how newly discovered lands outside Europe were to be divided between them. The line was drawn along a meridian 370 leagues, about 2,100 km, west of the Cape Verde islands. The lands east of the line were to belong to Portugal and the lands west of it to Castile. The line gave Portugal rights to the eastern part of present-day Brazil.

Around AD 400, two decorated horns of gold are made, probably drinking horns for religious use. The shorter horn has a runic inscription in which a man named Hlewagastiz says that he made the horn. The horns were found at Gallehus in 1639 and 1734, but were stolen and melted down in 1802.

At the Snartemo farm in Agder, men of high status are buried in large mounds during the Migration Period, 375–550. Two of the graves are among the richest men’s graves of the time in the Nordic countries, with swords with precious-metal fittings, splendid clothing, glass beakers and weapons. The graves were found in 1847, 1878 and 1933.

At the Levänluhta spring in Isokyrö, the dead are laid in the water during the Iron Age, between about 300 and 800, some 90–100 people in all. The waterlogged conditions preserved the bones unusually well, and the site is one of the oldest in Finland with preserved human bones. DNA from 13 of them shows that most had some Siberian ancestry, like other Finno-Ugric peoples.

text.en: The Finnish Heritage Agency’s register of ancient monuments gives burials in AD 300–800 and bones from about 90 people. English Wikipedia gives the 5th to 8th centuries and about 100 people.

summary.en: In 1420–1436 the dome over the cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore in Florence is built following Filippo Brunelleschi's solution. It was the first octagonal dome raised without a temporary wooden supporting frame, and it is still the largest masonry dome ever built. Pope Eugene IV consecrated the cathedral on 25 March 1436.

The area around the mouth of the Indalsälven river near present-day Sundsvall is unusually rich in finds from AD 200–600: gold, Roman imports, large burial mounds and weapon graves. A trading place grew up here, probably led by a chieftain or petty king. The elite grew rich from trade in iron, game, elk antler and furs, among other goods.

text.en: The Swedish History Museum’s text says that the trading place grew up in the 5th and 6th centuries, while the summary on the same page gives the 4th to 6th centuries. The finds in the area date from AD 200–600.

summary.en: Elephant birds were large flightless birds that lived only on Madagascar. Based on the youngest radiocarbon dates, a 2021 study suggests that the elephant birds and Madagascar's hippopotamuses died out sometime between 800 and 1050. At the same time people were changing the island's landscape, probably with fire, as forest became grassland, likely for cattle. Humans are thought to be the main cause, but there is little evidence that the birds were hunted.

caption.en: Eggs of the elephant bird Aepyornis maximus in the collections of the Muséum national d’histoire naturelle in Paris. Objects from Madagascar, photographed in 2020 at the museum. Detail. Photo: Marie-Lan Taÿ Pamart. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

summary.en: The mathematician and physicist Ibn al-Haytham, born in Basra, spent his most productive years in the Fatimid capital of Cairo. There, between 1011 and 1021, he wrote the seven-volume Kitab al-Manazir (Book of Optics). In it he explained that we see when light reflects from an object and reaches the eye, and that seeing takes place in the brain.

caption.en: Engraving on the title page of Opticae Thesaurus, a Latin edition of Ibn al-Haytham’s Book of Optics, in the Bavarian State Library. Among other things, it shows how Archimedes, according to the story, set Roman ships on fire with mirrors during the siege of Syracuse. The image belongs to the Latin edition and is not from Ibn al-Haytham’s time. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The Jewish philosopher and physician Maimonides, born in Córdoba, settled in Fustat in Egypt around 1168–1171 and lived there until his death in 1204. He was physician to Saladin and then at the Ayyubid court. Between 1185 and 1190 he wrote his main philosophical work, The Guide for the Perplexed, in Judeo-Arabic, that is, Arabic written in Hebrew letters. The work seeks to reconcile Aristotle's philosophy with Jewish theology. It was translated into Hebrew in 1204, was controversial in its day and also influenced Christian philosophers such as Thomas Aquinas.

caption.en: Page from a copy of Maimonides’ The Guide for the Perplexed, made by Ferrer Bassa in Barcelona in 1348, in the Royal Danish Library. The man on the chair with Stars of David is thought to represent Aristotle. The manuscript dates from 1348, not from Maimonides’ time. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: During the 11th century large groups of Bedouin from the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym tribes moved westwards from Egypt to the Maghreb. According to the traditional account, found for example in Ibn Khaldun, the Fatimids sent them to punish the Zirids of Ifriqiya, who had declared their independence, but many modern historians regard this account as Fatimid propaganda. How many they were is very uncertain: estimates range from a few tens of thousands to around one million. The migration was a major reason why the Maghreb gradually became Arabic-speaking.

A study of ancient DNA from 80 people shows that people of African and Asian origin began to form families on the Swahili coast around the year 1000, at the same time as Islam became widespread. In many of those buried in the coastal towns more than half of the DNA came from African, mainly female, ancestors and a large share from Asian ancestors. Of the Asian ancestry, 80–90 per cent came from men from Persia.

South-west of the Yoruba town of Ijebu Ode in south-western Nigeria runs a system of ditches with banks on their inner side, more than 160 km in all. They form an uneven ring around the old Ijebu Kingdom, an area measuring roughly 40 km from north to south. The earthwork is thought to have served defence and to have helped bring different communities together in one kingdom. Local legends link it to a wealthy widow, Bilikisu Sungbo, in whose memory it is said to have been built. When it was built is disputed.

text.en: The dating is disputed. The archaeologist Patrick Darling dated the earthworks to the 10th and 11th centuries, but more recent excavations point to the end of the 14th and beginning of the 15th century. Radiocarbon dates from the site go back as far as about 2000 BC, but that does not mean the ditch was dug then.

summary.en: At Igbo-Ukwu in south-eastern Nigeria, Isaiah Anozie found bronze objects while digging by his house in 1938. The archaeologist Thurstan Shaw excavated three sites in 1959 and 1964 and found more than 700 high-quality objects of copper, bronze and iron, among them ritual vessels, and about 165,000 beads of glass, carnelian and stone. The metal was of local origin, while many of the glass beads were probably made from glass from Mesopotamia and Iran, a sign of long-distance trade. The finds showed that such skilled metalwork had developed long before contact with Europe.

text.en: Thurstan Shaw dated the finds to the 9th century on the basis of radiocarbon dates he published in 1970. Newer dates are later: charcoal and wood from the Igbo Isaiah site were dated in 2022 to the 10th to 13th centuries, and a textile sample from there has been dated to 1027–1180.

caption.en: Bronze vessel in the shape of a snail shell from the 9th century, found at Igbo-Ukwu. Object from Igbo-Ukwu, photographed in 2013 at the National Museum of Nigeria in Lagos. Detail. Photo: Ochiwar. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: The settlement mound of Gao-Saney, seven kilometres from Gao in present-day Mali, is almost certainly the town called Sarneh in Arabic writings. People lived there from about 700. The finds show that in the 8th to 10th centuries the site traded in glass and copper on such a scale that, among known sites south of the Sahara, only Igbo-Ukwu has yielded more such traces.

caption.en: Gravestone of white marble with Kufic script, probably made in Almería in Spain in the 12th century and found at Gao-Saney. Object from Gao-Saney, in the National Museum of Mali, photographed in 2017 at an exhibition in Paris. From the 12th century, at the end of or shortly after the time of the event. Full image. Photo: Marie-Lan Nguyen. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

summary.en: When the Almohads under the caliph Abd al-Mu'min took Marrakesh from the Almoravids in 1147, they started work on a new great mosque that same year, according to the usual dating. The building standing today is a second, entirely new mosque from around 1158. Its 77-metre minaret was perhaps finished around 1195 under Ya'qub al-Mansur. The Koutoubia is counted among the most important buildings of Almohad and Moroccan architecture.

text.en: The usual chronology comes from French scholars in the first half of the 20th century and says that building began in 1147, the same year that Wikidata gives. A 2022 study by Antonio Almagro and Alfonso Jiménez reads the Arabic sources differently: according to it, building began in May 1158 and was finished the same year.

caption.en: Modern photo (2015) of the Koutoubia Mosque in Marrakesh, not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: Gedi is one of many medieval Swahili towns along the East African coast of the Indian Ocean, in present-day Kenya. The earliest evidence of settlement is a grave marker radiocarbon-dated to between 1041 and 1278, which places the founding in the 11th or early 12th century. The inhabitants adopted Islam in the 12th century, and three mosques were built one on top of another between the 12th and 14th centuries. The town lived on trade, had about 2,500 inhabitants at its peak and was abandoned in the middle of the 17th century.

caption.en: Modern photo (2007) of the ruins of the Great Mosque in Gedi, Kenya, not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: On the southern fringe of the Sahara, some 20 km north of the Niger River in present-day Mali, the site was at first used only at certain seasons. Early in the 12th century Timbuktu became a place where people lived all year round. The town's great role came later: after Mansa Musa's visit around 1325 the trade in salt, gold and ivory flourished, and Timbuktu became an important Islamic centre.

text.en: Leo Africanus wrote that the town was founded in 1213 or 1214 by Mansa Sulayman. Up to about the year 2000, archaeologists had found no remains from the 11th or 12th century within the modern town, since any such remains lie under several metres of sand.

caption.en: Timbuktu seen from a distance by Heinrich Barth’s party on 7 September 1853. Drawing by Martin Bernatz after a sketch by Heinrich Barth, printed in Barth’s travel account in 1857–1858, not from the time of the event. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The Great Mosque of Kilwa, on the island of Kilwa Kisiwani in present-day Tanzania, is one of the oldest partly surviving mosques on the Swahili coast. It was probably founded as early as the 10th century, but the first major building phase is the smaller northern prayer hall. In the 14th century the sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman extended the mosque to the south with a great dome.

text.en: The article on the mosque says in one place that the northern part was built between 1131 and 1170 and in another that it was built in the 11th or 12th century.

caption.en: Modern photo (2016) of the ruins of the Great Mosque of Kilwa Kisiwani, Tanzania, not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: Takrur was a state on the Senegal River in present-day Senegal that was at its height in the 11th and 12th centuries, roughly at the same time as the Ghana Empire. In 1035 King War Jabi introduced sharia and became the first ruler in the Sahel to officially adopt Islamic orthodoxy. He also waged a holy war against the king of Silla, subjugating its people and converting them to Islam. He died around 1040–1041. His son Lebi formed an alliance with the Almoravids against the Ghana Empire, and Takrur controlled trading posts on the route from the salt mines of Awlil on the coast to the interior.

The Zagwe dynasty was an Agaw royal house that ruled the northern parts of present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea from about 1137 to 1270, with its centre of power in Lasta. According to Ethiopian traditions, the dynasty's founder Mara Takla Haymanot overthrew the old royal line in 1137. The dynasty's best-known king is Gebre Meskel Lalibela, who is credited with the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela. In 1270 the last Zagwe king was killed in battle against Yekuno Amlak, who founded the Solomonic dynasty.

text.en: The Zagwe period is poorly known. Some king lists give eleven kings who reigned for 354 years, others only five who reigned for 143 years, and the historian Carlo Conti Rossini considered the shorter length the more likely. Wikidata gives the year 900 as the dynasty's beginning.

summary.en: At about dawn on 8 August 1303 the eastern Mediterranean was shaken by an earthquake, estimated at about magnitude 8, centred somewhere between Crete and Rhodes. The tsunami that followed caused massive flooding in Alexandria, where many ships were destroyed and some were carried up to about 3 km inland. Houses collapsed and many people died, most of the city walls were destroyed and the Lighthouse of Alexandria, one of the Seven Wonders of the World, was badly damaged. In Cairo minarets toppled, and much of the white limestone casing fell from the Great Pyramid of Giza.

text.en: The date 8 August 1303 is in the Julian calendar, which is the calendar Wikidata gives for it.

summary.en: The physician and scholar Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi, born in Baghdad, was living in Egypt when the Nile failed to overflow its banks. The missing flood caused a severe famine, and according to his detailed account the situation became so dire that many people turned to cannibalism. During the famine in the year 597 of the Islamic calendar (1200) he examined a large number of skeletons and concluded that the ancient physician Galen had been wrong about the formation of the lower jaw, the coccyx and the sacrum.

A 2025 study compares the dates of burials from South Africa's Iron Age with climate data. In north-eastern South Africa, carbon isotopes in baobab trees at Pafuri show that the Medieval Climate Anomaly, about 950–1250, was relatively humid, and the number of burials rose, especially around the Limpopo, where the state of Mapungubwe arose. After about 1300 the north-east also became drier, roughly when Mapungubwe was fairly abruptly abandoned, but researchers have long debated what role the climate played in that.

In the northern part of the Upemba Depression in the present-day Democratic Republic of the Congo, archaeologists have found nearly 200 graves in five cemeteries, among them Sanga. They date from the Early Kisalian phase (700–900) and the Classic Kisalian phase (900–1200). The grave goods of pottery, iron, copper, bone and ivory point to metalworking, long-distance trade and social hierarchy. Many customs of the Luba people, who live in the area today, can be traced back to this period.

caption.en: Reconstruction of a rich grave from the Classic Kisalian period at Sanga, with pottery, bones and metal ornaments, in the AfricaMuseum in Tervuren, Belgium. Photographed in 2019. Detail. Photo: Hispalois. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: The stela is a four-ton limestone slab from the Epi-Olmec culture. It carries about 535 signs in the Isthmian script and is among the earliest known written texts in Mesoamerica. Two Long Count dates correspond to May 143 and July 156, and the stela is dated by the later one. John Justeson and Terrence Kaufman have proposed a reading in which the text mentions, among other things, a solar eclipse and Venus, but other scholars, including Michael Coe and Stephen Houston, dispute it.

Towards the end of the Maya Late Preclassic period, between about 150 and 250, the Yucatán Peninsula was hit by drought. A 2022 study of pollen in lakes and lagoons in Mexico and Guatemala summarises that rainfall over most of the peninsula fell by at least 20 per cent compared with the preceding period, and that it was the most severe drought in the northern Yucatán in the last 2,000 years. The researchers argue that during the dry period maize became a way of coping with harsh conditions.

Pachacamac is an archaeological site of about 600 hectares in the Lurín valley, about 40 kilometres south-east of Lima. It is named after Pacha Kamaq, the ‘Earth Maker’, whom the coastal peoples here regarded as the creator god. According to the source, the site was settled around the year 200 and then flourished for about 1,300 years, until the Spanish arrived. Between January and April 1533 Hernando Pizarro travelled to Pachacamac and defiled the temple. The large religious complex is credited to the Lima culture, and in front of the temple was a raised space where pilgrims could leave offerings.

text.en: Wikipedia’s article on Pachacamac says the site was settled around the year 200. The article on the Lima culture instead says the complex was built and used from as early as about 200 BC until about 600.

summary.en: From about the year 1 to 500, Cahuachi was a major ceremonial centre of the Nazca culture. It lies on the south side of the Nazca River and overlooks some of the Nazca Lines. More than 40 mounds with adobe buildings cover about 1.5 square kilometres. For a long time researchers believed Cahuachi was the capital of the Nazca state, but few people lived there all year round. Instead, the site is now interpreted as a pilgrimage centre that many visited before and during major ceremonies. Newer research suggests that 40 of the mounds are natural hills reshaped to look built.

caption.en: Modern photo (2008) of the Cahuachi archaeological site in Peru, by Ed88, not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: In the mountains along the upper course of the Magdalena River in southern Colombia lies the largest collection of religious monuments and megalithic sculptures in Latin America, and the site is regarded as the world’s largest necropolis. The statues, thought to belong to the graves, show both humans and animals such as crocodiles, bats and jaguars, and the tallest is about seven metres. When they were carved is uncertain, but they are believed to date from about the years 5–400. Who made them is unknown, since the area is largely unexcavated.

text.en: The source says the age of the statues is uncertain. The span 5–400 is what is believed, not a firm dating.

caption.en: Modern photo (2020) by Bernard Gagnon of statues in Mesita A in San Agustín Archaeological Park, Colombia (file page). Indigenous heritage; the picture shows stone statues under a roof and no people. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: The Mogollon culture is the archaeologists’ name for a people of southern New Mexico and Arizona, western Texas and northern Mexico, whose culture according to the source takes shape around the year 200. The earliest villages consisted of a few deep pit houses, round or oval. Archaeologists recognise the culture by brown pottery built from clay coils scraped smooth, by its pit houses and by its own ceremonial buildings.

text.en: The source says the culture lasted until either about 1450 or 1540, when the Spanish arrived. The globe shows 1450 as the end year.

caption.en: View from Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument in New Mexico, photo from the National Park Service (unknown date). According to the file page the site shows homes of the Mogollon people who lived here more than 700 years ago, that is long after the beginning of the culture (about the year 200). Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The early Hohokam lived in small villages along the middle Gila River in present-day Arizona and grew maize and beans. Between about 300 and 500 a range of new crops was added, according to the source probably through trade with peoples in today’s Mexico: cotton, tepary beans and other beans, two kinds of squash and an amaranth plant. The Hohokam also dug canals to bring river water to their fields, and they later became known for their large irrigation systems.

Pinson Mounds in western Tennessee is the largest group of Middle Woodland mounds in the United States and was probably built around the years 1–500. On a plateau above the wetlands of the Forked Deer River are 17 mounds built wholly or partly by people, a semicircular earthen enclosure about 366 metres across and several habitation areas. The largest, Sauls’ Mound, is 22 metres high and the second-highest surviving prehistoric mound in the United States. Archaeologists believe the complex was built mainly for religious ceremonies, and several of the mounds contain burials.

caption.en: Modern photo (2007) looking across the top of Mound 10 at Pinson Mounds State Archaeological Park in Tennessee, by Brian Stansberry. According to the file page the mound was most likely a ceremonial platform mound. Not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY 3.0.

summary.en: Sometime between about 500 and 800, Taíno people from Hispaniola, Cuba or both began crossing the sea in dugout canoes to the Bahamas. Which route the first ones took is not known. Researchers have proposed voyages from Hispaniola to the Caicos Islands, from Hispaniola or eastern Cuba to Great Inagua, and from central Cuba to Long Island in the middle of the archipelago. The islands’ Indigenous people are known as the Lucayans. Some scholars count them as a branch of the Taíno, others do not. The Lucayans were the first Indigenous Americans whom Columbus met, in October 1492.

In the Llanos de Moxos, the seasonally flooded plains of the Bolivian Amazon, the Casarabe culture built a dense network of settlements over at least 4,500 square kilometres from about 400 to 1400. A 2025 study estimates that the population at its peak was between 10,000 and 100,000 people within an area of 5,020 square kilometres, and sees this as support for the idea that the culture lived in a kind of low-density city. Other researchers think a small population could have built the earthworks slowly over a long time.

text.en: The 2025 study says the culture existed from about 400 to 1400. Wikipedia gives 500–1400 in one place and 400–1400 in another.

summary.en: Glacier Peak is one of the five major stratovolcanoes in the state of Washington. Dating of ash layers and radiocarbon dating show that it erupted around the year 200, with an uncertainty of about 50 years. The eruptions that could be assessed rated 2–4 on the VEI scale, smaller than the 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens, which rated 5. The volcano’s largest mudflows, known as lahars, occurred about 5,900 and 1,800 years ago in connection with the growth of lava domes. Both times the mudflows travelled down the Skagit River all the way to Puget Sound.

caption.en: Modern aerial photo (2006) by brewbooks of the Glacier Peak volcano (3,213 m) in Washington state, seen from the south (file page). Not from the eruption around the year 200. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

summary.en: The El Molle culture lived in the Transverse Valleys of Norte Chico in Chile from about 300 to 700. It is known above all for its pottery. For a long time it coexisted with the Las Ánimas culture, which took over between 800 and 1000 and which may have learned copper working from the El Molle people. Several archaeologists, among them Grete Mostny, see links between El Molle and cultures of north-western Argentina.

The Tumaco-La Tolita culture lived on the coast of northern Ecuador and southern Colombia and is known for earthen mounds (tolas), pottery and above all metalwork. According to the source, its smiths were the first in the world known to work platinum. Because the metal melts at such a high temperature, they mixed platinum powder with gold or silver and made objects in white and yellow. On La Tolita island a village grew into a small town, and during the Late Tolita period, about 90–400, an estimated 5,000 people lived there. After that the island was abandoned, for unknown reasons.

A child from a group of hunter-gatherers who lived near present-day Ballito in KwaZulu-Natal was excavated in the 1960s. In 2023, researchers reported that they had found DNA from the bacterium Rickettsia felis in the child’s bones and had reconstructed the bacterium’s genome. It had been regarded as a new cause of human disease since it was first linked to illness in Texas in 1994, but according to the study it was present in southern Africa about 2,000 years ago, among people who neither kept livestock nor farmed.

A Greek medical treatise on acute and chronic diseases, written by Soranus of Ephesus in the 2nd century, is known today only through a Latin translation. It was made by Caelius Aurelianus, a physician and writer from Sicca in Numidia, present-day El Kef in Tunisia. In the few places where Soranus’s Greek survives for comparison, Caelius can be seen to keep to the wording of his model while leaving parts out.

text.en: Caelius Aurelianus probably worked in the 5th century, but some scholars place him two or even three centuries earlier. The later date is supported by his Latin, which has features of the Romance languages and resembles the language of Cassius Felix, another African physician who wrote around 450.

summary.en: Silphium grew only in a narrow area of the steppe in southern Cyrenaica, in present-day eastern Libya. According to Pliny the Elder, the last known stalk was found in Cyrenaica and sent as a curiosity to Emperor Nero, who reigned from 54 to 68. The plant is said to have died out in Roman times, and today no one knows for certain which species it was. Overgrazing and overharvesting have long been given as the causes, but more recent research argues that desertification was the main one.

caption.en: Object from Cyrene: silver coin from the 6th–5th century BC which, according to the file page, shows a seed or fruit of silphium, photographed in 2021. Where the coin was photographed is not stated. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Researchers have studied pollen, spores and charcoal in a sediment core from Marura Swamp on the Laikipia Plateau in Kenya. From about 2268 to 1615 calibrated years before present, the site was surrounded by dense montane forest dominated by Podocarpus. Around 1615 years before present, roughly AD 335, a mosaic of open woodland and grassland took over, and it still shapes the area today.
