According to the researchers, the shift may be linked to the spread of farming and herding, while the climate was changing as well.

According to the sources, dry conditions returned to parts of the Roman Empire under Emperor Hadrian, and Roman North Africa is said to have suffered five years of drought. The drought reportedly ended when Hadrian visited the region and rain finally fell again. The water shortage may have been one reason why Carthage was given a long aqueduct from the springs at Zaghouan, so that the city no longer depended on rainwater.

text.en: The sources give different years and places. The article on the Zaghouan aqueduct says the five-year drought ended with Hadrian’s visit in 128 and links it to Carthage. The article on the climate of ancient Rome says it rained for the first time in five years when Hadrian visited Timgad in 133. The years 123–133 cover both statements.

summary.en: The Canary Islands received their first permanent population about 1,800 years ago, sometime between the 2nd and 5th centuries. The settlers shared genetic, linguistic and cultural traits with today’s Amazigh (Berber) peoples of the Maghreb and probably came from north-western Africa. Afterwards the islanders lived with almost no contact with each other or with the mainland until European seafarers arrived in the 14th and 15th centuries.

text.en: As early as the 1st century BC, Roman fishers kept a seasonal camp on the islet of Lobos, where they gathered shellfish to make purple dye. According to the source, they did not live permanently on any of the islands.

caption.en: Modern photo (2016) of the almogarén, a ritual site of the islands’ Indigenous people, in the Cuatro Puertas archaeological area on Gran Canaria, not from the time of the event. Detail. Photo: H. Zell. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: Kirikongo in Burkina Faso shows how a small settlement in the bend of the Mouhoun River could grow during the Iron Age. It all began with a single household around AD 100. Four centuries later several families lived there in earthen houses with clay floors, and none of them seems to have ranked above the others. Over time the village grew to thirteen mounds covering 37 hectares, and people lived there until about 1700. According to the source, the area belonged to the ancestors of today’s Bwa.

The first Roman commander to take troops across the Atlas Mountains was Gaius Suetonius Paulinus, in 41. He had just become governor of the Roman province of Mauretania, in present-day northern Morocco, and had put down a revolt there together with Gnaeus Hosidius Geta. His account of the mountain country survives through Pliny the Elder, who quotes it in his Natural History.

According to several ancient geographers, baboons and other live animals were among the goods sold in Adulis, the Aksumite port town on the Gulf of Zula on the Red Sea, about 40 kilometres south of present-day Massawa in Eritrea. From the 1st to the 7th century AD the town was a busy trading centre. Pliny the Elder is the first European to mention it, and the sailing guide known as the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea lists ivory, hides and slaves among the goods shipped from there.

In the first half of the 2nd century the Romans built an aqueduct that carried water to Carthage from springs in the Djebel Zaghouan, about 60 kilometres south of the city. Including all its branch channels it was 132 kilometres long, among the longest in the Roman Empire. The water was moved by gravity alone: over a little more than 90 kilometres the channel dropped 264 metres, and the water took a day and a half to two days to arrive. The aqueduct could deliver between 17 and 32 million litres a day. A sacred fountain building with a crescent-shaped portico was erected over the main spring.

text.en: When the aqueduct was built is not entirely clear. The source names two events that may have prompted it: Emperor Hadrian’s visit in 128, when a five-year drought is said to have ended, and the opening in 162 of the Baths of Antoninus in Carthage, which needed more water than rainfall could supply. The range 101–150 follows the source’s statement of the first half of the 2nd century, so the year 162 falls outside it.

summary.en: Martianus Capella was a jurist and learned Latin writer in Roman North Africa. He wrote his only known work, De nuptiis Philologiae et Mercurii (On the Marriage of Philology and Mercury), after Alaric’s sack of Rome in 410, but apparently before the Vandals conquered North Africa in 429. Among the wedding gifts for Philology are seven maids, the seven liberal arts: grammar, dialectic, rhetoric, geometry, arithmetic, astronomy and harmony. The work greatly influenced how learning was organised in Europe right up to the 12th century.

text.en: According to Cassiodorus, Martianus came from Madauros, the birthplace of Apuleius, but this is considered unreliable because Martianus’s own autobiographical passages say that he came from Carthage. The point is ancient Carthage.

summary.en: Terracotta figures of riders, the oldest known in the Niger region, are among the finds of the Bura culture in the lower Niger valley, in south-western Niger and south-eastern Burkina Faso. Radiocarbon dates place the culture from the 3rd century AD to the 13th century. The dead lay beneath terracotta vessels and wore quartzite beads, brass nose rings and bracelets of iron or brass. Hooked iron arrowheads have also been found. Because the sites only became known in 1975 and excavation began in 1983, the culture is still poorly explored, and how it relates to later kingdoms is unclear.

caption.en: Object of the Bura people in Niger: terracotta grave marker from the 3rd–11th century, in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. The whole image is shown. Licence: CC0.

summary.en: The Garima Gospels are ancient manuscripts in Ge’ez, the language of the Kingdom of Aksum, containing all four Gospels. Radiocarbon dating gives the older manuscript, Garima 2, an age of about 390–570 and the younger one, Garima 1, about 530–660. Garima 2 is believed to be the oldest surviving complete illustrated Christian manuscript, with pictures that include portraits of the Evangelists. Before the dating, Western scholars thought the books came from about 1100 or later.

text.en: According to the monastery’s tradition the books were written by Saint Abba Garima, who is said to have arrived in Ethiopia in 494, and tradition places the first two close to the year 500. In one place the source describes the radiocarbon result for Garima 2 as the 6th century, but the range it gives is about 390–570.

caption.en: Illumination from the Garima Gospels, 6th century according to the file page. The event (the year 390) and the file page's dating give different times; the caption follows the file page. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The Confessions is Augustine’s account of his own life, written as prayers addressed to God. He wrote the thirteen Latin books between 397 and 400, shortly after becoming bishop of Hippo Regius, present-day Annaba in Algeria, in 396; he stayed there until his death in 430. In the Middle Ages many Christian writers followed its example, and Henry Chadwick has called it one of the great masterpieces of Western literature.

How many people lived in the Han Empire? The chronicle known as the Book of Han has preserved much of the census that the Western Han carried out in AD 2. It arrived at 57,671,400 people in 12,366,470 households. The figure covers only families that paid tax, because the state wanted to know what revenue and how many soldiers it could count on. Modern scholars consider the count to have been fairly accurate.

Silt in the Yellow River settles on the bottom and raises the water year after year, and in AD 11 the embankments no longer held. The river broke through in Wei Commandery and found a new way to the sea past Pingyuan and Jinan, the second major recorded change of course. The floods were among the things that brought down Wang Mang’s regime.

The Chinese knew of a great empire far to the west that they called Daqin, and in AD 97 the general Ban Chao sent his subordinate Gan Ying to find out more about it. Daqin was the Roman Empire. Gan Ying reached Tiaozhi by a great sea, and the chronicle Hou Hanshu says that no one before him had got so far. There, Parthian sailors talked him out of sailing on: with good winds the voyage took three months, but with contrary winds it could take two years, and seafarers used to bring food for three years. Gan Ying gave up and turned home without having seen Rome.

text.en: Where Gan Ying turned back is not certain. The chronicle names Tiaozhi, which is interpreted as Characene on the Persian Gulf, and the article on relations between Rome and China says the Persian Gulf. The article on Gan Ying leaves open whether the “Western Sea” he reached was the Persian Gulf, the Black Sea or the eastern coast of the Mediterranean.

summary.en: Ivory, rhinoceros horn and tortoiseshell were what the strangers brought with them when, in AD 166, they entered the Han Empire at the frontier of Rinan, in the far south. They said they had been sent by Andun, king of Daqin, that is, Rome. The name fits the emperors Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, but Antoninus Pius had already died in 161. The chronicle Hou Hanshu writes that the two empires then had direct contact with each other for the first time. Several historians believe they were Roman merchants rather than an embassy from the emperor.

text.en: The article on Rinan says the embassy came from Marcus Aurelius. The article on relations between Rome and China says it is unclear who sent it, since both emperors were named Antoninus, and that they were probably merchants rather than diplomats. Neither source says exactly where on the Rinan frontier they entered; the point at Huế lies in the area that belonged to Rinan.

summary.en: In December AD 185 a new light appeared in the southern sky, in the asterism the Chinese called the Southern Gate, between Alpha and Epsilon Centauri. The astronomers wrote that it was the size of half a bamboo mat and showed changing colours. The light gradually faded and disappeared in the sixth month of the following year, after about eight months. The record in the chronicle Hou Hanshu is believed to be the oldest surviving description of a supernova.

text.en: Researchers have interpreted the record in different ways, from a supernova to a distant, slow-moving comet. According to the source, later X-ray measurements with Chandra point to a Type Ia supernova.

summary.en: The physician and philosopher Ge Hong collected remedies for acute conditions in a handbook, and in it he recommends sweet wormwood, Artemisia annua, against recurring fevers, a typical sign of malaria. The Chinese scientist Tu Youyou noticed that the water was to be cold, because hot water destroys the active substance, and so she tried extraction at a low temperature. This led to the discovery of artemisinin, which was rewarded with part of the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

text.en: The article on Tu Youyou says that Ge Hong wrote the book in 340. The article on Ge Hong gives no year for the book and states that he died in 343 or 364.

summary.en: Under Diocletian, Nicomedia was the leading capital of the Roman Empire in the east, until in 330 Constantine chose nearby Constantinople instead. On 24 August 358 a powerful earthquake shattered large parts of the city, and what was left standing was laid waste by fire. Nicomedia rose from the ruins, but the new city was smaller than the old one.

Far south of Galilee, at Petra in present-day Jordan, the damage was devastating when two powerful earthquakes struck one after the other on 18 and 19 May 363. That same year the Temple in Jerusalem was to be rebuilt on the orders of the emperor Julian, but the work never happened. Ancient historians such as Sozomen pointed to the earthquake as the cause; today it is also noted that the change of ruler after Julian’s death may have halted the plans.

In the Hermitage in Saint Petersburg stands a large limestone slab from the desert city of Palmyra in Syria. On the stone, which dates from the 2nd century, the city recorded how much duty different goods cost when they were brought through Palmyra and which officials were in charge of trade. The text is written in both Greek and Palmyrene and is the longest Canaanite or Aramaic inscription on stone ever found.

caption.en: Column 1 of the Palmyrene Tariff (the tax law of Palmyra), dated to the 1st–2nd century AD according to the file page. An image of the inscription; the file page names no photographer. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: A shipload from Muziris in southern India was worth about 9 million sesterces. The cargo, above all pepper and other spices, was brought home on the Roman merchant ship Hermapollon, and we know of it through a Greek papyrus from the 2nd century. The papyrus contains a contract between a financier and a merchant in Alexandria who imported the goods. Although only parts of the text survive, it has become an important source on how trade and loans were regulated in antiquity. Muziris was known for its spice trade with the Middle East and the Mediterranean world.

text.en: Where Muziris lay is disputed. For a long time the port was placed in the Kodungallur area, but excavations at Pattanam since 2007 have led some scholars to favour that site. That identification is also contested.

caption.en: The verso of the Muziris Papyrus (P.Vindob. G 40822), a Greek papyrus document from the mid-2nd century AD in the Austrian National Library; according to the file page the verso contains a list of the Indian cargo of the ship Hermapollon, including Gangetic spikenard. The papyrus is dated somewhat later than the year of the event (101). Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: How can iron stand outdoors for more than 1,500 years without rusting away? That question has made the pillar in Delhi famous among archaeologists and materials scientists alike. It is 7.21 metres high and 41 centimetres in diameter, weighs more than six tonnes and was made under King Chandragupta II, who reigned around 375–415. The iron contains a lot of phosphorus, and an even, crystalline layer of iron phosphate has formed on the surface that protects it from Delhi’s climate.

caption.en: The iron pillar in the Qutb complex at Mehrauli, Delhi, photographed in 2007. Cropped. Photo: Sujit kumar. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: Nearly 1,800 characters in Classical Chinese cover all four sides of a granite stone in Ji'an on the Yalu River. It is carved from a single block, about 6.4 metres high and almost four metres round. The stone was set up in 414 at the tomb of Gwanggaeto the Great, king of the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo, on the orders of his son Jangsu. Ji'an was then the capital of Goguryeo but today lies in north-eastern China. The inscription is among the most important sources for the history and myths of Goguryeo, and how it should be read has become a point of dispute between the countries of East Asia.

The burial mound Daisen Kofun in Sakai is 486 metres long and surrounded by a moat. It is the largest of Japan’s kofun and is thought to have been built over about 20 years in the middle of the 5th century. Who lies there cannot be established, but it is usually counted as the tomb of Emperor Nintoku, and the Imperial Household Agency of Japan treats it as such. From the late 3rd century to the 6th century more than 20,000 such mounds were raised over Japan’s rulers, and the era has been named the Kofun period after them. Since 2019 Daisen Kofun has been part of the Mozu–Furuichi World Heritage Site.

caption.en: View of the Daisen Kofun (Daisenryō kofun, "the whole tomb" in the file page's Japanese description): the forested tomb mound can be seen at the edge of a city. Modern photo (2018) by Saigen Jiro; a burial mound (monument), no remains. Licence: CC0.

summary.en: Seven stone pillars with inscriptions in Sanskrit have been found by the Mahakam River on Borneo. They are called yupa, sacrificial posts, and were made during the reign of King Mulavarman. The texts tell that he gave the Brahmins thousands of cattle and large amounts of gold, and they name three generations of rulers: Kudungga, his son Aswawarman and his grandson Mulavarman. The name Kudungga is not Sanskrit, and he is assumed to have been a local chief. The inscriptions are regarded as the earliest known evidence of Indian influence in the Malay world, and the kingdom of Kutai as one of the first in Indonesian history.

text.en: The article on Kutai dates the script to the second half of the 4th century and calls it Pallava script. The article on Mulavarman says he reigned around 400 and calls the script Brahmi. The pillars were found at the mouth of the Kaman; the point is Muara Kaman, where the kingdom’s capital is thought to have been.

summary.en: The oasis city of Loulan by the lake of Lop Nur was an important stopping place on the Silk Road as early as the 2nd century BC. The kingdom had already been renamed Shanshan in 77 BC, but the town kept the name Loulan. When the Tarim River, which gave the town its water, changed its course, there was probably too little water left, and by 330 the town stood empty. Today Lop Nur has dried up entirely, and the ruins lie in the middle of the desert.

The dryness of the desert has preserved a man who was buried on the Silk Road about 1,700 years ago. He was found in 1995 and was unusually tall, about 1.9 metres, and around 30 years old when he died. His face was covered by a white hemp mask with a golden diadem, and he wore a woollen garment embroidered with naked putti, goats, bulls and pomegranate trees. Radiocarbon dating gives the years 245–385.

In Gyeongsan in south-eastern Korea, archaeologists have since 1982 investigated more than 1,600 graves of a local elite in the kingdom of Silla. The graves were built over about 100 years between the 4th and 6th centuries, and in many of them sacrificed people followed the grave owner in death, a custom that according to historical records was banned by the king in 502. Five people had parents who were closely related, both among the grave owners and among the sacrificed, and genetically the two groups could not be told apart.

text.en: The article says in its introduction that the graves date from the 4th to the 6th century, but in the methods section that they were built between the 4th and the 7th century.

summary.en: Lake sediments and cave stalagmites show that the climate in the Sasanian Empire became much drier around 480. Yet the empire grew and farming expanded in those same years. The researchers think that qanats, underground channels that carry groundwater and so cope better with dry years, together with varied and flexible farming may have softened the effects. The authors stress that climate data from the region still have large gaps.

The monastic rules available in China were incomplete, and so in 399 the monk Faxian, around 60 years old, set out from Chang'an to fetch scriptures from India. He travelled west along the Silk Road, entered India from the north-west and stayed there for about ten years, among other places in Pataliputra. His account of the journey is an important independent source on Buddhism in India at that time.

caption.en: First page of Faxian's travel account (Record of the Buddhist Countries), a 12th-century woodblock print. According to the file page the first sentences tell that Faxian in Chang'an decided to go in search of more Vinaya texts in the year 399/400. A later print, not from Faxian's time. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: When Afghan mujahideen were digging a trench on top of an artificial hill at Rabatak in 1993, they found a stone with text in Bactrian written in Greek letters. The inscription dates from the 2nd century and concerns the emperor Kanishka, who according to the text received the kingship from Nana and all the gods and who inaugurated year one. The stone gives important information about the line of the Kushan dynasty.

The Romans built a mill complex at Barbegal outside Arles. Water from an aqueduct drove 16 wheels standing in two parallel rows along a steep hillside. No larger mill installation from antiquity is known. The mills may have ground several tonnes of flour a day and worked from the early 2nd century until towards the end of the 3rd.

A bronze plaque made in Roman Gaul in the 2nd century, probably towards its end, carries a calendar in Gaulish written in Latin letters. It follows both moon and sun in a five-year cycle of twelve lunar months a year plus two inserted months. About 40 per cent survives. The plaque was found in 1897.

In the second half of the 1st century the Romans began large-scale gold mining at Las Médulas. At least seven long channels brought water there to make the mountains collapse, a method described by Pliny the Elder in 77. The site became the most important gold mine of the Roman Empire and left a striking landscape.

The Tower of Hercules is a Roman lighthouse from the late 1st century, perhaps built or rebuilt under Emperor Trajan. An inscription names the architect Gaius Sevius Lupus from present-day Coimbra. The tower was restored in the 18th century, and no other Roman lighthouse is both fully preserved and in use today.

The bridge at present-day Drobeta-Turnu Severin was the first over the lower Danube. Designed by Apollodorus of Damascus, it was built in 103–105 so that troops could reach Dacia. At 1,135 metres long it rested on 20 masonry piers carrying wooden arches. It functioned for only 165 years; parts of the piers survive.

On 6 February 131 a wax tablet was written that is the earliest known mention of Alburnus Maior, today’s Roșia Montană in Transylvania. The Romans founded the place under Trajan as a mining town, with settlers from Illyria. Mine galleries, tools, cemeteries and 25 wax tablets have been found there.

In 67 Emperor Nero himself broke the ground with a pickaxe for a canal across the Isthmus of Corinth. About 6,000 prisoners of war from Judea dug from both sides, but the work was abandoned when Nero died shortly afterwards. According to Suetonius they managed to dig about 700 metres. The modern canal follows the same route.

The bog of Vimose in north-west Funen has yielded some of the earliest Elder Futhark inscriptions that can be dated. A comb from about 160 carries the word harja and is considered the oldest datable runic inscription known. Most of the other objects with runes date from about 200–300.

text.en: The marker stands at the bog of Vimose, about 10 km north-west of Odense according to Lex and Wikidata's entry for the bog. English Wikipedia and Wikidata's entry for the inscriptions give a point in the centre of Odense, without a source for it.

summary.en: Around 400 a round stone fort was built at Eketorp on Öland. It is thought to have been a refuge in case of attack and a place for religious ceremonies. At first it was about 57 metres across. In the next century the wall was moved out to about 80 metres, with some fifty small rooms and buildings in the centre and in the wall. The fort was abandoned in the mid-7th century.

Finds at the Roman palace at Fishbourne show that fallow deer were brought to southern England in the 1st century. In Roman times people spread the fallow deer across much of Europe. The British population died out after the Roman period, and new animals were later brought there from Anatolia.

A young man buried at Great Chesterford between 415 and 545 had lepromatous leprosy. Lipids and the bacterium’s DNA confirm it. It is so far the earliest radiocarbon-dated case in Britain confirmed in both ways, and isotopes suggest that he probably came from a place outside Britain.

At Driffield Terrace in York a cemetery from the 2nd to the 4th century was excavated, where an unusually large share of the dead had been decapitated. Researchers have sequenced the DNA of seven of them. Six resemble today’s Celtic populations of Britain, especially in Wales, while one man has affinities pointing towards the Middle East.

At Fallward near the North Sea coast a man was buried in an oak boat more than four metres long in the second quarter of the 5th century. The grave goods showed Roman influence, among them carved furniture and a military belt. His DNA shows that he carried the leprosy bacterium and that he may have come from a population on the Roman frontier.

The Drumanagh headland has a large Iron Age promontory fort where Roman coins, ornaments and pottery have been found, and in 2025 the first intact Roman pot in Ireland. On nearby Lambay Island there were graves with Roman brooches of a style found in Roman Britain from the late 1st century.

text.en: Researchers disagree about what Drumanagh was. Some think the fort was a bridgehead for a Roman invasion, others a Roman trading post or an Irish settlement that traded with Roman Britain. The site has not yet been properly excavated, and the dates rest on the finds from Lambay.

summary.en: A sediment core from the seabed in the Gulf of Taranto shows how the climate varied in southern Italy. After a warmer spell the temperature fell sharply from about 245 and reached its lowest around 265–275, a level not reached again until about 518. The cold and dry period coincided with the Plague of Cyprian.

In the eruption of Vesuvius in 472 the ash travelled as far as Constantinople, more than 1,200 kilometres away, where ashfall was reported. The eruption was sub-Plinian and thus smaller than the one that buried Pompeii in 79. Eruptions of that size have recurred more often than the large ones, a few hundred years apart.

Researchers have sequenced the DNA of 37 people from two Gothic-associated burial sites dating from about 320–489: Aquae Calidae near Burgas and the Aul of Khan Omurtag near Shumen. The dead were not a single population. The Goths in the Balkans seem to have formed from migration, alliances and peoples on the Roman frontier.

Ambrym in Vanuatu is a large basaltic volcano. Around the year 50 it had a huge Plinian eruption, which left behind a caldera about 12 kilometres wide. The eruption has been given a value of 6 on the VEI, the scale that measures how explosive volcanic eruptions are.

For about 600 years, from around the year 60, people were buried in the sand dunes at Sigatoka. Isotopes in bones and teeth show more food from the sea than at other burial grounds in the southwest Pacific. Earlier studies of the skeletons suggest good health and adequate nutrition.

All of the at least 58 eruptions that Taveuni in Fiji has had since people settled there have struck the southern two thirds of the island. After major eruptions between about 300 and 500 the southern part was abandoned, and it remained deserted until about 1100.

text.en: The years 300–500 and 1100 rest only on one sentence in Wikipedia's article on Taveuni, and that sentence has no reference of its own. The study the article is based on (Cronin and Neall 2000) is not freely available and could not be opened.

summary.en: Dated corals on twelve islands in French Polynesia show that sea level fell by an average of 0.3 mm a year between 3,600 and 1,200 years ago, but unevenly. Large microatolls from 1,600–1,400 years ago suggest that it then stood almost still. Traces of storms are most frequent 2,500–1,500 years ago.

text.en: The study gives the ages in thousands of years before present but does not say which year it counts from. The years here are counted from 1950 and may be off by a few decades.

summary.en: A chicken bone from a stone-lined post hole at the Kvarnbo settlement on Åland is radiocarbon dated to 266–541. It is the oldest directly dated chicken find in Finland. The bird had a maternal lineage missing in the study's other ancient chickens. Chickens from Sweden may have helped make Åland's chickens different.

At Kroggårdsmalmen in Karis the dead were buried unburnt in the early Roman Iron Age. The graves are square stone frames split into cells for one or two people and covered by low stone mounds. This type, the tarand grave, is common in Estonia and northern Latvia. The site seems to have served only a few generations.

Around the year 200 a community that both traded and made goods arose on the island of Helgö in Lake Mälaren, some five centuries before Birka. The place lived on into the 9th century. Finds show that skilled craftsmen were already working gold here in the 5th century.

Melting ice patches in Jotunheimen and the nearby mountains have yielded over 2,000 finds, many from reindeer hunting. Radiocarbon dates of 153 objects show that dated finds rise quickly around the 3rd century. At the same time, archaeology shows permanent farming settlement spreading in the mountain valleys of Oppland.

In the 1st century a man was buried in a wooden coffin at Hoby on Lolland. With him lay a Roman table service from Italy, including two silver cups with scenes from the Iliad. His teeth suggest he was local. The service has been read as a sign that a local elite copied Roman drinking customs.

In Lithuania horses were buried from the Roman Iron Age until Christianisation in 1387. Sixteen horses from the 3rd–7th centuries, from six burial sites, averaged 130 cm at the withers. They were unusually large compared with the Viking Age horses there, which averaged 124 cm, but small next to horses in central and western Europe.

The Chernyakhov culture existed from the 2nd or 3rd century to the 5th century in today's Ukraine, Moldova and Romania. People stayed in fixed places and lived mostly on grain, and tools for tilling and harvesting are frequent finds. Amphorae from the Roman Empire among the finds point to trade contacts.

text.en: Wikipedia says the culture flourished between the 2nd and 5th centuries. A genetic study from 2026 instead gives the mid-3rd to the early 5th century.

summary.en: From the 4th to the 7th century the Imenkovo culture existed on the Middle Volga. Its people ploughed with iron tools and grew barley, wheat and rye; they also kept livestock and made pottery and metal goods. Its techniques influenced neighbouring Finno-Ugric groups. Which people carried the culture is disputed.

caption.en: Reconstruction (model) of a semi-dugout house of the Imenkovo culture after V. F. Gening and P. N. Starostin, in the National Museum of the Republic of Tatarstan in Kazan. Modern photo (2018) by Engelberthumperdink. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: Emperor Claudius had a 5.6 km tunnel dug through Monte Salviano to keep down the level of the Fucine Lake and lead part of its water to the river Liri. According to Suetonius the work needed 30,000 workers and took eleven years, from 41 to 52. How well the tunnel worked is uncertain.

Baiae was a Roman resort on the Gulf of Naples. Bradyseism, slow ground movements in the volcanic area, lowered the coast below sea level, apparently in two phases: between the 3rd and 5th centuries and more a century later. Early in the 4th century, water began to cover a palace there.

In the mid-5th century at least 47 children up to three years old were buried in the rooms of a decaying Roman villa near Lugnano in Teverina. DNA of the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum has been found in one of the children, and research suggests that many of the dead were victims of malaria.

The Roman country house Villa Romana del Casale in Sicily was built in the first quarter of the 4th century. One room later received a new mosaic, laid over the original floor, showing women in athletic contests. The villa's mosaics include women athletes whose two-piece outfits look like today's swimsuits.

When Edmund Ironside died on 30 November 1016, the West Saxons accepted Cnut as king of all of England. Under an agreement made on an island near Deerhurst, Cnut was to inherit the whole kingdom on Edmund's death. Cnut later also became king of Denmark in 1018 and of Norway in 1028, and England became part of the North Sea Empire.

text.en: The sources differ on the coronation: English Wikipedia says that Cnut was crowned in London in 1017 by Lyfing, Archbishop of Canterbury, while Swedish Wikipedia has the North Sea Empire begin when he was crowned in 1016.

summary.en: On 14 October 1066 William of Normandy defeated the English king Harold Godwinson near Hastings, where the town of Battle stands today. Harold was killed in the battle. William was crowned king of England in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066, and the battle began the Norman Conquest of England.

text.en: The date is in the Julian calendar, which was in use at the time. Wikidata gives the same day (20 October in the Gregorian calendar).

summary.en: Bishop Magnus I consecrates the cathedral in Turku on 17 June 1300 to the Virgin Mary and Saint Henry. The stone church stood where an older wooden church had been, and it was enlarged in the 14th and 15th centuries. Today it is the mother church of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Finland.
At the farm of Stiklestad in Verdalen a peasant army loyal to Cnut the Great defeated King Olaf Haraldsson, who was killed in the battle. Olaf later became the patron saint of Norway.

text.en: The date of 29 July 1030 is traditional. English Wikipedia mentions that a solar eclipse occurred on 31 August of the same year, which does not fit that date. Wikidata also gives 29 July 1030.

summary.en: Around 890 the chieftain Ohthere of Hålogaland visits King Alfred in England and tells him about life in the north. His wealth came mainly from the tribute the Sámi paid in furs, hides, feathers and ropes of whale or seal skin. He said he owned 600 tame reindeer.

text.en: The source only says that Ohthere lived in Hålogaland. Suggested sites lie near Tromsø, for example Senja, Kvaløya and Malangen, so the marker is approximate.

summary.en: In 834 two women are buried in an oak ship just over 20 metres long, in a mound on the Oseberg farm in Tønsberg. The grave had been robbed, but it still held a four-wheeled wagon, sledges and household goods. The year comes from the tree rings in the timber of the burial chamber. The mound was excavated in 1904.

In the early 1130s a wooden stave church is built at Ornes on the Lustrafjord; the tree rings show that the timber was felled in the winters of 1129–1132. The builders reuse parts of an older church, including a carved portal from around 1070–1080 that gave its name to the Urnes style. The church is a World Heritage Site.

In 1349 the Black Death reaches Norway on a ship from England that docks in Bergen. During 1349 and 1350 the plague spreads to Stavanger, Trondheim and Eastern Norway, among other places. An estimate based on abandoned farms puts the population around 1500 at a little over 60 per cent below its level before the plagues.

From around 1350 until 1754, North German merchants of the Hanseatic League run an office at Bryggen in Bergen. Dried fish from northern Norway is traded there for grain from Europe. The buildings of Bryggen are a World Heritage Site today.

According to Landnámabók, Ingólfur Arnarson sailed from Norway and settled in Reykjavík in 874. He is regarded as the first permanent settler in Iceland. By tradition the Age of Settlement, when the settlers took possession of the land, lasted until 930, and Landnámabók names 430 settlers.

text.en: Wikipedia and Landnámabók give the year 874. Store norske leksikon writes that Ari the Wise’s Íslendingabók gives the year 870, and calls that date the better founded. Both saga works were written down only in the 12th and 13th centuries.

summary.en: At the Althing in 999 or 1000, Iceland becomes Christian. The lawspeaker Þorgeir Þorkelsson, accepted by both sides as mediator, decides the matter. The pagans keep some concessions: horse meat may be eaten and private pagan worship is allowed, but the Church later bans them.

text.en: Tradition gives the year 1000, but some historians give 999, according to Wikipedia. Store norske leksikon writes 999/1000. The oldest account is in Ari the Wise’s Íslendingabók.

summary.en: After years of civil strife in the Age of the Sturlungs, Iceland’s chieftains agree to pay tax to King Haakon IV of Norway. In return the Icelanders are to receive a law code, peace and reliable shipping with Norway. The agreement, Gamli sáttmáli, ends the Icelandic Commonwealth.

text.en: Wikipedia dates the agreement to 1262–1264; Store norske leksikon writes that Iceland submitted to the Norwegian king in 1261–1264. Both have the Commonwealth end in 1262.

summary.en: The Danish king Valdemar II and his crusaders defeat non-Christian Estonians at Lindanise, the site of present-day Tallinn. The victory helps Valdemar take northern Estonia. According to a later legend, the Dannebrog, a red flag with a white cross, fell from the sky during the battle.

Reval, today Tallinn, joins the Hanseatic League and becomes its northernmost member. The Danish king had granted the town Lübeck city rights in 1248. The Old Town, with its medieval and Hanseatic layout, has been on UNESCO’s World Heritage List since 1997.

The town law of Haapsalu from 1294 is the first written mention of the Swedish population in Estonia. From the 13th to the 15th century many Swedes came from Finland to Estonia’s coasts and islands, such as Ruhnu, Vormsi and Noarootsi. Haapsalu was the centre of the Estonian Swedes until 1944.

Estonians in Harju County and on the islands of Saaremaa and Muhu rise against their German and Danish overlords and against the Livonian Order. The uprising is crushed. In 1346 Denmark sells the Duchy of Estonia to the Teutonic Order for 19,000 Cologne marks.

In 1201 Bishop Albert moves the seat of the Livonian bishopric from Ikšķile to Riga, where the Livonians already lived, after forcing the elders to agree. The year counts as the city’s founding. In 1202 the Livonian Brothers of the Sword are founded, and German crusaders conquer the land in the 13th century.

From 1282 Riga is a member of the Hanseatic League, the league of trading towns around the Baltic Sea. The town founded by German crusaders 81 years earlier becomes one of the league’s ports, and Riga is still described today as a former Hanseatic town.

Kernavė on the Neris, 35 km from Vilnius, is first mentioned in writing in 1279 and is counted as Lithuania’s first capital. The knights burned the town in 1390. The area was sparsely inhabited as early as the end of the Palaeolithic, and the site became World Heritage in 2004.

In a letter of 25 January 1323 to German cities such as Lübeck and Bremen, Grand Duke Gediminas invites merchants, craftsmen and peasants to Lithuania. The letter is the first written source to mention Vilnius, and the year is counted as the city’s founding. By then at the latest, Vilnius was the capital.

Grand Duke Jogaila is baptised in Kraków in 1386. After his return the nobles and peasants are baptised, first in Vilnius and its surroundings, and in 1387 a cathedral is built in Vilnius on the site of a demolished pagan temple. Samogitia is the last to be Christianised, in 1413. Lithuania was the last state in Europe to be Christianised.

text.en: Store norske leksikon dates the Christianisation to 1386, the year of the personal union with Poland. Wikipedia describes the baptisms in Vilnius as starting after Jogaila’s return and gives 1387 for the cathedral. The event is placed in 1387.

summary.en: Grand Duke Vytautas moves Karaims from Crimea to Trakai in 1397 and 1398, after a campaign against the Golden Horde. The Karaims of Lithuania have a language of their own, Karaim, and their wooden synagogue, the kenesa, stands in Trakai. In 2021, 192 people in Lithuania identified as Karaims.

text.en: Wikipedia’s article on Trakai gives 1397 and 1398. According to the article on the Crimean Karaites the move rests on Karaim tradition, in which the legend first gave 1218. The Karaim of Lithuania differs greatly from that of Crimea, and some historians doubt that the Lithuanian Karaims came from Crimea.

summary.en: In 122, under Emperor Hadrian, Rome begins a wall across the whole island, 117 km from Wallsend on the Tyne to Bowness-on-Solway. Forts, milecastles and turrets with soldiers lined it. The wall lies wholly in England and has never been the border with Scotland. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1987.

Pope Gregory the Great sends the monk Augustine with about 40 missionaries to convert the Anglo-Saxons. In 597 they reach Kent, where King Æthelberht lets them preach in his capital, Canterbury. The king is baptised before 601. The Celtic bishops of the Britons refuse to accept Augustine’s authority.

On 18 July 1290 King Edward I issues an edict expelling all Jews from the Kingdom of England before All Saints’ Day, 1 November. They may take cash and belongings, but their debts owed to them, homes and communal buildings go to the Crown. They were perhaps about 2,000, but estimates vary.

A letter from Scottish nobles to Pope John XXII, dated at Arbroath on 6 April 1320, asserts that Scotland is an independent kingdom and asks the pope to lift the excommunication of King Robert the Bruce. It was probably written in Arbroath Abbey. The surviving copy bears 19 seals.
